utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner, Selma Sakic, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing that we need turn our minds to, the -- we'll lower the blinds so that the witness can be escorted back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. You -- you well know the procedure by now, but I'm obliged, for the record, to remind you before Mr. Cvijetic resumes his cross-examination that you're still on your oath. You may resume your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This morning we'll go through two topics that I believe are relevant, and you've discussed them partly in your examination-in-chief with the Prosecution. I'd like to show you a document from our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 811. Tab 4. I'm sorry, I made a mistake. We need 65 ter 10501, and it's 1D365. 1D365; it's in the Prosecutor's folder, tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is a document the Prosecution has already shown you, and this is the cover letter for the document we will open. It says that thereby attached is an instruction on how to handle the civilian affairs in the crisis areas, and it's signed by Major-General Milan Pujic. Since you discussed this document, I would just like to turn to the next page to see what is stipulated there. It defines the tasks of the civilian authorities in the commands of the JNA and local commands, and we'll move to the next page immediately to see what it looks like, and then I'll ask my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We won't go into details because you've done that with the Prosecution already. Just let's read the subheading. Tasks from the area of state administration, legislative, judicial and executive authority. In December 1991, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence specified in greater detail that the civilian affairs organs in military units would have in the areas that I've just read out. You said you had not had occasion to read this document before, when the Prosecutor asked you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were shown exactly what these tasks were, and it says that military units, in their respective areas of responsibility, especially during combat operations, have certain powers to take over the role of civilian authorities if these civilian authorities are not operating in your area of activity. Is that written here?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document for the first time in my contacts with the Prosecution here at The Hague Tribunal. The first time I was invited, around the 6th of September. When I was a military commander, I never saw that document, nor acted upon it. By reading this document and another attachment to it, I saw that these affairs and activities were brought down to the brigade level so that civilian affairs organs were activated up to brigade level but not lower.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't go into detail because you've done that with the Prosecutor already. Just let me ask you: If, in your area, civilian authorities are not functioning, can that, in any way, affect the combat readiness of your brigade and interfere with the execution of combat missions?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all areas where I executed combat operations, civilian authorities were functioning properly so I never encountered this situation. Let me just add one thing. In the process of preparing for this second stage of testimony, I came across information that, at the corps level, General Talic issued an order appointing a civil affairs organ, and that was Colonel Vojin Vojunovic [as interpreted]. I also found that he based his activities in some municipalities in Krajina, for instance, in the municipality of Kljuc. In the area of activities of my brigade, he never showed up, and he never dealt with such issues, and I have to emphasise, once again, in my area of activity, all the civilian authorities were functioning properly. So there was no need for anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you just repeat the name of that commander appointed by General Talic?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Gojko Vojnovic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll move onto the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 10502.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I -- before I -- before we move on, first of all, it would helpful if Mr. Cvijetic would agree that the document in question was not shown first to the witness in September, when he came here, but is referred to in the statement that was made on the 30th of -- of August -- August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In the transcript the 8th of September, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, no. No, Your Honours. He said he first saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But he didn't, that's what I'm saying. And I'm asking Mr. Cvijetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. sorry. I misunderstood that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, no. He was shown it and dealt with it in the last paragraph, paragraph 18 of the statement that he made. And I see the witness nodding. And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I think we can deal with it easily by asking the witness. I will accept any answer he gives.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. What the Prosecutor is saying is true. I made a mistake because my interview was somewhere at the beginning of September, and that's when I was first shown it. I got confused for a moment between two different periods.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. And at the moment, it's not exhibited. But perhaps, as you've been asking questions about it, we can have it made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's already exhibited. 1D365.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D365.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see Judge Delvoie and I are somewhat surprised by that. It's certainly not on my list as an exhibit, this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know exactly through which witness it was exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said the 65 ter number, but it has an exhibit number, 1D365.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Smith agrees, it didn't appear either on your list or my list, as we gave it an extra outside the -- the -- the range of 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we will move on to 65 ter 10502.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm trying to establish the basis and the origin of that previous document on the basis of what it was adopted. Here before you, you have an instruction for conducting civil affairs in crisis areas. Just let's turn to the last page to see who passed -- who adopted this instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, the last page but one. The last page but one; that's one before this. This is the last page. Now we need the one before. This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And we'll stay on this one. Can you just confirm that this instruction was issued by the Federal Secretary for National Defence, Army General Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see a signature here. I don't see -- I don't -- I can't know that it's Veljko Kadijevic's signature. I see it has no stamp. But I can say the same as before. I have not -- in fact, I did not see it at the time, nor did it ever have any effect at any level below the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you just read the second paragraph on the page you're looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can zoom in on the second paragraph for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you see, General Kadijevic prescribes that in areas where civilian authorities are not functioning, pending the establishment of civilian authority, certain steps can be taken by the military. Is it, indeed, what it says?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it now, and before, and I have already given an answer. That applies to areas where civilian authorities were not functioning,

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Could you just look at the last paragraph but one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think from line 18 through to 25 needs to be redacted. We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. We can move on and in the future we will not mention the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you read para 12?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Let me ask you the question. The federal secretary allows for the possibility that a commander improvise on the spot and adapt to the situation on the ground, so this document has the nature of an instruction, giving authority to the commander to decide on the ground on what measures would be appropriate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you for this warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as you have observed, I am aware of that and as soon as I think that we need to go to private session I will request that. But I think that is not necessary yet. Let us go back to document -- 65 ter 886.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, I -- I stand to be corrected if I'm wrong, but I don't think this document that you have just been asking the witness about has been exhibited. If I'm wrong, could somebody please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I can tender it and since it is in the context of the previous document I seek to tender it, as I think it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, obviously I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D388, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we see 65 ter 886.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, we'll deal with this briefly. You say -- or, rather, you commented on this document which was signed by Lieutenant-Colonel Branislav Grujic. And it's an order about the establishment of the defence of the town of Donji Vakuf. As you have just spoken about Derventa and Brod, here, too, military persons were appointed to high posts in the civilian structures, including the judiciary, and so on. Do you not think that the military commanders in this municipality, Donji Vakuf, identified the reasons as outlined in that document and that they have taken over these posts, in accordance with the documents that we've seen?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have provided an answer to this matter yesterday, and I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You doubted the authenticity of the document, but I must warn you that we cannot doubt documents on the 65 ter list. And I must treat this document as authentic. So I asked you about the contents of the document. We heard your opinion about its authenticity. So do you agree with my conclusions that these military commanders actually realised their authorities and in the municipalities without functional civilian structures, military persons were appointed to responsible posts in the civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry for the interrupting the interpreters. Can the witness fairly be expected to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is one of the type of questions that I've been objecting to, "Do you agree with my conclusions?" He can put a proposition to the witness but not in that form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You can try again, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, I put it to you that the military commanders who signed this document acted in accordance with the powers bestowed on them, and the document I showed you, and they appointed military persons to high-ranking persons in the civilian structures. Do you agree with what I'm saying? And was it, indeed, the case?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree. Because can I only be responsible for my own acts and not the acts of the commander who drafted this document. Why don't you call him and have him answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that such an order was issued and that it was in force in the municipality of Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, that I have commented this order. This order is illegal, starting from the stamp and all through the end. It's dated the 19th of June. At that time, military stamps of the JNA were no longer valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. You explained as much yesterday, so we don't dwell on this document anymore.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can -- I'm sure, redact the last ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I don't necessarily deem it necessary at this point. I don't know what the rest of your question is. Perhaps it doesn't create a problem. It's for you to indicate, because you would know where you are going.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honours. I will not mention the witness's name. I will deal with a document. Could we please see document 1D04-3091.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you are familiar with this document and that you have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is this document the type of document that you, as a commander, would rely on most while commanding your unit? And is it a document that you should be best familiar with?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of the rule-books that is most important to me for successful control and command. But there are other rule-books too. I have one on me. I showed it, and activities were more or less carried out, pursuant to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this has an English version. Oh, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think we should move into private session at this point to deal with this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours. Let me just correct the transcript in -- on page 13, line 19, I mentioned order -- I said issue orders and what's recorded here doesn't make much sense.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours. And the document is admitted as 1D389.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the next document, 1D00-0272.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is a regular combat report sent to the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Date: 14 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see page 2. The page before this. I'll have to provide the ERN number. ERN ... this is the page, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness, in this regular combat report, it is stated that in the Prijedor Tactical Group, there are volunteers and the police, among other members. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the end of that paragraph, at the bottom, they are given deployment and assignments. Assignments are also given to the volunteers and the police. That's the last sentence. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we see the page before this. It has the page number 2; ERN 0086-1633. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Look halfway down the page, where it says: "Operations Group Doboj." Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You can see that this operations group also includes a battalion of the MUP and a tactical group.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, page number 4, ERN 0086-1635. I think that's the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, can you see where it says level of combat morale, and it describes the heavy losses sustained by a company of reserve police that was involved.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's just look at the last page to see who signed this document. Who signed this? Look to the left. Obviously one of the officers signed for General Talic, one of the officers of the 1st Krajina Corps. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the stamp of the 1st Krajina Corps, but whose signature this is, I don't know. It's obviously not the signature of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: No dispute about that. Can you agree with me that this is a regular combat report sent, as we can see from the heading, to the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that's at the corps level. The corps is reporting to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to conclude that members of the police were also engaged as part of units of the corps with certain assignments?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment on -- on what General Talic wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You don't have to comment. I'm asking you if it's obvious from the report.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This battalion from the MUP that is mentioned as part of the Operations Group Doboj, I don't know which battalion it is, and for that reason I can't say anything. I can't say what it was all about, and which unit was involved. It would be very thankless for me to comment on the reports sent by my superior further up the chain. I did not see any of these reports, and I'm not prepared to give a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is there any reason to doubt that this report is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason to doubt or confirm.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, really, that is, if I can put it, a non-question question. I mean, the witness has said he knows nothing about this report, he hasn't seen it before, and it is no good Mr. Cvijetic trying to get it in by saying, Is there any reason to doubt its accuracy? Although, can I say, if he wants to have it admitted, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honours, I must say I can't help noticing that in his testimony the witness doubts the authenticity of certain documents whose authenticity is really beyond any doubt. But, of course, whatever the Trial Chamber decides. If you want me to, I'll withdraw my question and move on. I will, though, ask that this document be admitted as extremely relevant, in view of the Defence's case concerning the engagement of police units in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't follow this at all, I am afraid. I mean, Mr. Cvijetic is really making a speech here. But there's never been in this dispute that police units were fighting. The question is how they came to be there. That's the only question of dispute and this document doesn't assist on that at all. And that's the issue between the Defence and the Prosecution, not the fact that police were engaged in combat operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Hence, Mr. Cvijetic, if there is no issue as to the fact of police units being engaged in combat operations, is it necessary to exhibit this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document mentions something else that I did not refer to yet. You can also see the line of engagement of the police in military operations, and that's an exclusively military line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I assume that, like the previous two documents that were admitted, the -- there being no objection by the other side to tendering them, although the witness has no personal knowledge of them, the relevance is that they go to establish system and method. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I actually wanted it in for a completely different purpose, which I'm going deal with in re-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D390, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The next document is 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you proceed, Mr. Cvijetic, and I'm addressing both counsel, the Court Officer needs to be instructed as to whether it is the -- an instruction from the Chamber, depending on what the parties say, whether these three exhibits should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think so. Well, I suppose it's a question of --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is no need, because even the witness's unit is not mentioned, let alone the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we see no need either for them to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a -- 2D46. Here, can you see the command of military post, certain number, order for further operations. And can you see, in the second paragraph, that the military police and a platoon of civilian police also received assignments by this military order, and a directly military assignment was given to the platoon of civilian police. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's just look at the last page to see who signed this. We can't see whether it's a lieutenant-colonel or a colonel, but the last name is Samardzija. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I think this answers the objection to my previous document. The question was on whose orders they were engaged in military operations, and here we can see that. Do you agree that an officer with a rank of a commander of the military P.O. box - it's probably a brigade - orders the police to take part in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your leave, I need some more time to answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you see the stamp?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a regular municipality stamp, not a military stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In the heading of the document it says military P.O. box command, Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the witness wanted to give an answer to the question he was asked. So could we have the answer. The question was: "Do you agree that an officer with a rank of commander of the military orders the police to take part in combat operations?" And the witness wanted to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if this was interpreted correctly. It was not military police commander. It was commander of a military P.O. box. Let's just see on the first page again which unit it was. Left-hand top corner.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, can I see that. I don't know that military P.O. box. It was not one of my neighbours. That commander had command only over military police, not civilian police, and I explained that extensively in my interviews with the Prosecution and in my prior evidence. And one of the answers I've given is that we had both trained and untrained commanders. Obviously a trained commander would have never written an order like this, and would never have affixed a stamp of a civilian organisation on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The point of my question was that he did make such an order and he did engage the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer only for my own actions in the post I occupied. What other people did, I really cannot be expected to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. This line of questioning had one purpose only. You have just said -- or, rather, stated your version of the participation of the civilian police in combat operations upon the question of Ms. Korner, and I will put the position of the Defence to you, which you may accept or not. Here it is: The armed forces of the former Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia consisted of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, as well as any individual who volunteers and goes to the nearest draft office and accepts the rules of military hierarchy and discipline. In the RS, instead of the JNA, the Army of the RS stepped in, and with the Territorial Defence and with the volunteers, it made up an armed force. The police could participate in the execution of combat activities but only pursuant to the rules of resubordination to the military command in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the position of the Defence. I will end by asking the witness whether he agrees with our position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There were at least three separate questions rolled up into that. I think this must be broken down. The first question is -- just a minute, please, Mr. Cvijetic, and will you see my objection. Whether he agrees that the armed forces of the former Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia consisted of the Yugoslav People's Army and the Territorial Defence, as well as any individual who volunteers. That's the first question. Second question: In the RS, instead of the JNA, the Army of the RS stepped in and with the Territorial Defence, and with the volunteer it made up an armed force. That's the end of the second question. Third question: Could the police participate in the execution of combat activities but only pursuant to the rules of resubordination? So that is three separate questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you remember those questions, or did you need to have them repeated by Mr. Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a very broad topic about which I would have to speak for another day, possibly. This has to do with the constitutional matters, the Law on the Armed Forces, the rule-book of service in the army, and so on. This would require us to go back to these matters and see whether they stand or not. But I have put forward my definitive position. I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I accept that. I will repeat my question broken up into smaller parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The armed forces are a whole and consist of the Yugoslav People's Army, the Territorial Defence, and the members of the armed forces. Correction: A member of the armed forces is any citizen, who with a weapon in his hand, or without it, participates in resisting enemy forces. That's how it was regulate in the former SFRY. So I ask you if you agree that this is correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now here's my second question: In war, during imminent threat of war and in other extraordinary circumstances, the police can be used to carry out combat operations of the armed forces in accordance with the law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instruction on the use of the Territorial Defence says that in war, the police is an integral part of the TO. Item 6 of the instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And, now, during the time it carries out combat operations of the military -- of the armed forces, the police is subordinated to the commander who manages the combat operations in question.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a unit is attached to such a military unit and subordinated to it, then it carries out relevant tasks. But a condition for that is that everything be legal and covered by orders, legislation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This is what I have just read out from the regulations setting -- laying this out. Thank you, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, just one follow-up question. The way the previous question was put to you and the answer you gave to me, make me wonder, it is not the fact of executing combat operations that subordinates a unit to the military, if I understood you correctly, but it is the subordination to the military that permits a unit to be in combat operations. So it's the other way around, if you see what I mean. You first have to be subordinated before you go into combat under military command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: (redacted). I did not report to the MUP organs because, as we said yesterday, Mr. Zupljanin, as chief of the Banja Luka CSB, to which that police belonged, and the entire brigade staff were -- were members of the police. So it would have been superfluous for me to inform Mr. Zupljanin additionally, because he was kept up to date daily through his -- through the members of his police units. That unit, as an infantry brigade that was part of a corps, did not carry out tasks from the remit of the civilian police, and that's why the police wasn't informed either. And, anyway, there were people from the CSB who reported along professional lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, in other words, the CSB in Banja Luka was kept informed at all times about the activities of the brigade while it was resubordinated to the corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know how the reporting was done? Did the police officers that you had under you, did they report in writing, or did they send daily combat reports or whatever name these reports might have had? Do you know how they reported back to Mr. Zupljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how they informed him. Perhaps through personal contacts, because Mr. Zupljanin was there. Maybe Mr. Zupljanin, along the lines of control and command, informed his minister or any other superiors. I don't know that. But the people who were there, who most of them were inspectors of the MUP and they were in constant contact with Mr. Zupljanin and there was no need for drafting additional reports as we had people present constantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we're at the point where we would take the usual break. So we would lower the blinds so the witness could be escorted from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And before -- before we rise, we have been made aware of the concerns of the support staff as to the inconveniences caused by the irregular extensions to the indicated breaks, so we would ask everybody to be back after 20 minute, as we would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You may be seated, sir. Yes, Ms. Korner, whenever you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I just want to deal with some of the matters you were asked about in cross-examination. First of all, you were asked by Mr. Krgovic, and this is at page 16218 following, about the process of disarmament in Kotor Varos. And it was put to you that roads had been cut by members of the opposing forces in -- in Kotor Varos. And I just want to put this in context by looking at a map, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have up on the screen, it's part of the map book, and it is 10137.2, which was at tab 61 of our documents. Your Honours, I'm not at all clear at the moment, really, what the status of the map books are, whether they have been given exhibit or not as a whole, but at some stage we better try and sort is out, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: As I recall, when we last visited this question, I had myself expressed some doubt on the area and I had been corrected in my assumption up to that point, that -- that the entire book had been or would have been exhibited, but it was pointed out to me that from the time we would have started, separate pages had been individually exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And -- and I think having started out down that path, we must continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think probably the answer is, Your Honour, when we filed the bar table motion if we can just throw in the maps that have not already been exhibited as part of that and rather than starting to work out which one are in and which ones aren't yet. Right. Have we got that up? It is 10137.2. All right. Can we sort of focus on Kotor Varos, and I just want to look at the municipalities that Kotor Varos was surrounded by again. Kotor Varos would be where we see YK, if we can focus in. Yeah, thank you, will do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, so Kotor Varos was bordered, first of all, by Celinac, as we can see. To your knowledge was Celinac virtually a completely Serb majority -- I mean, sorry was a Serb majority municipality?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no clear Serb majority in Celinac. I cannot give you the percentages, I don't know how many Bosniaks there were. But as far as I know, the village of Mehovci and Gornji Celinac and perhaps some other places were populated predominantly by Muslims. But, again I cannot give you any percentages. I would have to consult statistics. There were Muslims though. I don't know of any town or village populated by Croats though so there was a negligible number of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the answer is you don't know. Don't worry, we will deal with it through a different route. What about Skender Vakuf? Do you know what the percentages there were?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skender Vakuf, there were two Muslim villages, and the other places were predominantly populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Teslic?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Teslic, there were more Muslims and Croats than in the other two municipalities. I cannot give you the exact percentages without statistics, but the majority population were Teslic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, the majority population is -- sorry. The majority population has come out as Teslic. Did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipality of Teslic, as far as I know, the Serbs were the majority population, followed by Muslims and Croats. They were a bit more numerous, but I again cannot really provide percentages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So the only -- in Travnik was what, largely; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Travnik, the Croats and Muslims were the majority, and the Serbs were the minority. Again, I cannot give you the exact share in the population of any group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As a military man, would it be your assessment, then, with the exception of Travnik, in fact, Kotor Varos was surrounded by areas where the Serbs were in a majority?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's difficult to say. Well, yes, if you take municipalities and compare those. And the Serb population there. But Kotor Varos itself was rather heterogeneous if we speak about villages and towns inhabited by Serbs, Croats, and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I'm going to, in fact, next show you a more detailed map of Kotor Varos which is part of the map bundle again. I think it may have been exhibited though.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, that's a -- a breakdown of the municipality by villages and with the overall majorities in those villages being shown, and we can see also that part of Teslic and Skender Vakuf and, indeed, Celinac appear on the map. Can I just ask you: Are you aware of any disarmament operations being carried out in the village of Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maslovare, like in all other settlements, was a place where integrated actions were carried out. They were no different from other populated centres. Disarmament was carried out all over the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm specifically referring to Maslovare. Are you aware of any disarmament operation by the police or the military taken against the village of Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Maslovare village, the population was predominantly Serbian. When I said it was carried out a moment ago, I meant Siprage. I got a bit confused. But Maslovare was populated predominantly by Serbs and most of those people were already in the Army of Republika Srpska, but the operation applied to the whole territory of the municipality, so in Maslovare, equally, if somebody had weapons illegally in their possession, they were supposed to be disarmed, like anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... suppose being the operative word. Well, you mentioned Siprage, hasn't come up clearly on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we move the map up a bit and can you see Siprage on there. No, up, upwards. Sorry. All right. Downwards, I suppose then. I want Siprage which you can see at the bottom of the map. Okay. Don't bother. I don't think it's worth the trouble.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Siprage -- yes, yes, go on. That's good. Thank you. Stop. In fact, as we can see, and you have mentioned it was a largely Muslim village; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Siprage was predominantly Muslim, but there were Serbs living there as well. So it was a mixed population. Still, with a Muslim majority.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, sir. That's all I'm going to ask about that aspect. Now, Mr. Krgovic showed you a map which allegedly showed the positions of the opposing forces, and I believe that was ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We better have it up on the screen again. I think it was -- Mr. Krgovic, correct me if I'm wrong, it was 2D07-1171. Is that -- oh, he's gone, so he can't correct me if I'm wrong. All right. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. The wrong translation is showing. That's for the next map that I'm going to show the witness. Well, it shouldn't be. It's got nothing to do with it. Yep. Now, I don't -- I don't need to bother about the translation. That can go off the screen so we can try and get the map the right way around. Okay. Oh, is this the one we couldn't get the right way around. I wonder if Mr. Aleksic could hand his over. Okay. I tell you what, if he hasn't got it, I will hand my copy over and we can put it on the -- and we can put it in Sanction. Oh, it is in Sanction. If we can go to Sanction. If you can turn the witness's thing to Sanction. Yes, thank you. Has it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, can you see the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. If you turn it into Sanction. If you switch the Sanction thing on. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you ever seen this particular document before? You were shown it by Mr. Krgovic yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it yesterday for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Is this in the format that the military maps that would have been produced in 1992 would have been produced?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the military regulations, levels of command are strictly stipulated for map making. As far as I can see, the scale is 1:100.000, but in my brigade, all graphic instructions were done on a map, 1:50.000. That's what the regulations stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This one appears to say, if you look at the side, this is 1:50.000. It may well be that the simplest thing is I'd like you to have a look, please, at a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is simply being done to show what, we suggest, were the military maps that were produced at the time. It was disclosed to the Defence, it comes from the 1st Krajina Corps documentation that was seized in 1998. Can we have up, please, on the screen -- right, again in Sanction. We'll leave it in Sanction, it's quicker. 10553. And there -- the last translation that suddenly came up on the screen should go with this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, have a look at that, if you can see it, and tell us, first of all, whether this is the type of military map that was produced in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the kind of map that belongs in the category of general map, because there are decisions written into the map, but there are general-view maps that are intended to show the situation in general. I see this as a general map, not a tactical map, defining the decision of the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we -- can we -- is it possible to have the translation of what's written on it by the side or not? Okay, we can do that in -- in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Sir, just so that everybody understands the writing on it, is it headed decision of the command -- commander of the Light Brigades group, military secret. And then approved, Major-General Momir Talic, strictly confidential?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm terribly sorry, but we are facing a problem trying to follow in Serbian, the -- what -- what Ms. Korner is -- is reading from. Because it's -- it's very small -- small print on the map, and, therefore, we would need that part enlarged in order to be able to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That part -- that's a good point. I'm not sure exactly where that is on this writing. If you focus, please, on the bit in the middle. Yep. At the top. No. This is going to be a rather tedious and time-consuming exercise, I feel.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I want to know, sir, can I put it this way: The maps that were produced by the corps or -- or -- under which you came, as a military man, were they all in this sort of format, with handwriting on it?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maps are normally made by hand and drawings are made by hand. We have to get one thing clear. This concerns a group of brigades. I see here Petar Spasojevic as the commander. This is to be approved, according to the rules, by the corps commander. We cannot see the signature of General Talic, that he approved the map. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this map, I don't see that the decision was, indeed, approved by Corps Commander General Talic or that are it was signed by Petar Spasojevic. So, to me, this is a general-view map. And a general map is meant to be viewed by anyone who comes into that conference room.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. But all I'm trying to get at is, sir, is that the military maps in use in 1992, whether an overall map like this, or one that deals with the particular area would be handwritten, there would be handwriting on it, and it would be authorised by the -- the corps commander; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. All maps - that is, decisions - are to be approved by the superior. And they are all done in hand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I ask. And I'm not asking -- the map has no relevance in itself. So I'm not asking for it to be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Next ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, quite, Your Honours. At the moment we've had no explanation of what these maps are or how they are produced, and I'm trying to show that the maps that were actually in use do not look like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, we're talking about the maps from two opposing sides, so this witness can give evidence on the maps which are in use in the Serbian army, and this is -- this is the opposing army, so -- the opposing army map, as far as I understood. So I don't see how we can generalise on the -- on the contents and the way how the maps were produced on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. My understanding was this was allegedly the map produced by Mr. Krgovic. And I see Mr. Pantelic and Mr. Aleksic, sorry, sitting there. It is meant to be a map showing from the Serb side, Bosnian Serb side, nothing to do with the opposes forces. It's meant to be showing the opposing forces, and I understand that -- it seems to be the suggestion is this is map that comes from the time and we don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm wrong and maybe Mr. Zupljanin Defence can provide with us the explanation because I understood quite contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, we are speaking about this map under the -- that Ms. Korner just made a reference 2D07-1171. On the top right part of that map, there is a clear sign that it was issued by the government of Republika Srpska in Bosnia, Republican Secretariat for the Relation with the ICTY. So it is obviously that it's from the archive of this body, whether it's made by the military authorities or not. If -- if necessary, we could take a look on it, but the basis is that a certain position of enemy forces under the command of Raif Alagic on the date of 11 of June, 1992 was, at that time, in the region of Kotor Varos. So we really don't know if that is in dispute, this position or former one, you can ask witness and I think he gave quite detailed answer. And frankly, I mean, it's not so important issue. I mean, it's not in dispute between parties that the clashes were on in Kotor Varos and -- June 1992, and simply as that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are a number of different points. The first is my understanding was that this was produced absolutely by this organisation in Banja Luka as a representation of a genuine map that was produced at the time to show the position of the alleged opposing forces. And if you will recall, I asked for information about that. And I didn't get any because Mr. Krgovic doesn't know one way or the other, and I'm -- all I'm trying to show at this stage, and we'll make our own inquires, is that the maps are different. And the witness has dealt with that. As to the rest of Mr. Pantelic's suggestions, there is an issue -- not that -- that there were not resistance in Kotor Varos but as exactly how many and how they were described. However, I've dealt with that point. So if we could move on, please, to a different matter but arising from the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You spoke about Mr. Sadikovic and the book that he wrote. And you volunteered that he said that he had under him five detachments, namely, the 5th Detachment, the 35th, 55th, 84th and 105th. And according to all the establishment regulations, detachments normally have up to 500 men. I don't know if Muhamed Sadikovic had as many men. Now, that's information, is it, sir, that you obtained from his book?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some of that information even before the execution of combat operations, but not the details of where each detachment was located, what its name was and what its part of the assignment was. I got confirmation after the operation, concerning these details, from the book, from the author, Sadikovic, in the annex, appendix to the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you, of course, knew Mr. Sadikovic, didn't you, because you were engaged in the negotiations for Mr. Sadikovic and his men to surrender?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see ... [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, page 39, lines 19 through 23, the witness's answer was not quite correctly interpreted. Could the witness repeat? I think he said something different so that I don't have to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, I had the same note from my B/C/S speaker as well, that it wasn't correctly interpreted. Which -- the answer from lines 19 through 23 on the previous page. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, I -- I'll go back over this. I was asking you whether the information you gave the Court yesterday at page 16236, to 26 [sic] of the transcript about Mr. Sadikovic came from the book and your answer was: I had some of that information even before the execution of combat operations but not the details of where each detachment was located, what its name was and what its part of the assignment was. I got confirmation after the operation concerning these details from the book, from the author, Sadikovic, in the annex, appendix to the book. Now apparently that isn't a correct recording of what you actually said. Is there anything that you want to correct in it?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said and I stand by it. There's nothing to change. I saw Mr. Sadikovic for the first time on the 7th of April, 1992. And as for these detachments, I said yesterday, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am really sorry. Perhaps we can listen to the tape. The witness said: I had all the details where the units are, where they are located but I didn't have the numbers, what each unit's -- what each detachment's number was. So he had all the information. He just didn't have the numbers of the detachments. These are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told, Your Honours, that the translation came out as "details" but it was "numbers." That's -- that was the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I'm going ask you one more time about this. But are you sure that you didn't take part in the negotiations that led to the surrender of Mr. Sadikovic and his men?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in talks with various structures. But directly concerning the surrender of Sadikovic and his men, I did not take part in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Now, sir, you did some researches, as you told the Court, and when you came with the documents, before you came back here, and one of the documents we noted that you had got was the report by the military analyst, Mr. Brown, and I'll come back to that in a moment. Did you, yourself, download that from the Internet; if not, how did you get hold of it?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know do it myself because I do not have Internet access. I got this at the department for co-operation with the ICTY, and they had downloaded it from the Internet and it was meant as mere information for me to know what he had written. Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will come back to that in a moment. I want to stay with Mr. Sadikovic for a moment. Were you aware that Mr. Sadikovic had testified in the case against Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you had been aware, in the light of your researches, would you have asked for a copy of that testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. -- Ms. Korner, the questions, if so-and-so, always likely to be unhelpful and I suspect that appears to be the case with this question. I don't know where you can go with --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't pursue that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told the Court today that Colonel Vojnovic had been in charge of morale, and you discovered that, though you weren't aware of it at the time. Did you get that from Mr. Brown's report?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Vojnovic was one of the commanders assistants and that was his responsibility. But he was responsible for that for a very short time. And in my zone, he never approached me about this, so I never really learned about this until I was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I want to know is -- I'm just trying to get at what you, yourself, actually personally knew at the time or afterwards or what you got from Mr. Brown's report. Because that may be important. Now, is that something that you learned from Mr. Brown's report?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw in Mr. Brown's report that Mr. Vojnovic used to go to Kljuc, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that because Kljuc was way outside my zone. But I read that in that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Korner. Sorry for interrupting. There is a constant mistake and it might turn out to be important. It is recorded as Mr. Vojnovic with O, V-O, and all the time the witness is talking about Mr. Vujnovic. Which is V-U, Vujnovic. So this should be corrected in the whole transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. Zecevic. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, all that I want to know is what was the purpose of your obtaining from this so-called centre for co-operation a copy of Mr. Brown's report, and how did you know about Mr. Brown's report?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about it at all. They mentioned it to me. They said they had such a report downloaded from the Internet, and that I was free to read it, to get acquainted with it. But I didn't ask for it because I didn't even know about it. I received another book that was a monography about the VRS. I was given that to read it, and it speaks about the establishment of the army and all the dates, and so on. I got these two books as kind of axillary reading, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did this so-called centre know that you were a witness here?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they knew. But they -- the -- the people know me. And we spoke about this in general terms, and they merely mentioned they had such a book so I could take it and read it for my information with no special purpose in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did they give you anything else at all?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They only gave me a book about the VRS, the first volume. It was published on the anniversary of the establishment of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is any of the evidence that you have given here over the last -- earlier and in the last two days, is any of that simply based on what you read in Mr. Brown's report or the history of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no special differences there. All I have said so far matched that. There may have been minor differences in some details. Possibly some regular combat report to the command corps where something is mentioned, but I have seen many of these reports here already so that basically there is nothing new there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to -- to move to -- thank you. I want to move a slightly different topic and that's this: You were asked about Lieutenant-Colonel Stevilovic, who was killed in Kotor Varos in July. And it was put to you, in terms, that he had a special unit that was also operated in Kotor Varos, and you said you had never heard such a thing before. Just ask you a little bit more about Stevilovic and the military police. He was -- you told us he was the colonel in charge of the 1st Krajina Corps's intelligence and security. Did that mean he was in charge of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the security organ. The intelligence organ is something else. He was the security organ, and he was chief of the Department of Security in charge of the use of the military police of the 1st Krajina Corps. There was a battalion of the military police, and he was in charge of it as an establishment unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, can you just tell us, what -- was there any difference in the uniform between what a military policeman wore and what a regular member of the army or police wore? What, if anything, would distinguish them as a member of the military police.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, those military policemen only wore white belts. And the rest of the uniform was the same as that of all other soldiers. So the only difference were the white belts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to show you a clip of a video because there's a number of different video -- uniforms and I want to see if you can help us with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a video that's been disclosed but wasn't on our 65 ter list, but I simply want to show it to the witness because it's a good mixture of uniforms. It's 10555. And it was disclosed with the other videos that were obtained from Banja Luka on the 10th of August. We can --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I believe that this line of questioning by Ms. Korner does not emanate from the cross-examination, so I see no grounds for dealing with this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this arose not out of the Mr. Cvijetic's cross-examination but out of Mr. Krgovic's. So I don't know what Mr. Cvijetic is doing on his feet in the first place. It was specifically put to the witness that at the same time as the special police from Banja Luka were operating, Colonel Stevilovic's, men were operating as a special unit. The witness has denied it, but I think it is important that we see, as he has described, the difference between the types of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to say that having regard to the evidence we have heard over the past months, in terms of this uniform and who is wearing what, if this video is useful to -- to eliminate -- to -- not eliminate, sorry, to illuminate that -- that the -- the issues that have arisen there, although it may not have strictly arisen out of cross-examination, this witness could be of assistance. He should be permitted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, the date, I think, appears at some stage on the screen. It's August of 1992. Yes. 10th of August, 1992. And for what it's worth, the video shows that it's a place called Karanovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know where Karanovac is?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karanovac is a village which is at the place where the road to Knezevo diverges from the main road, Banja Luka-Jajce. It is from 15, 20 kilometres from Banja Luka, southward in the direction of Jajce. That's where the road to Knezevo diverges. There's a bridge over the Vrbas river and that's where the village of Karanovac is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. We'll just play this video, if you'd like to look at it, and we'll pause because I want you to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can we stop and look at this man. Are you able to say what sort of uniform that is.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which uniform do you mean? What the police officers are wearing? Because there are two kinds.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you can tell us, the man in the centre of the picture, wearing a white shirt and what appears to be blue trousers and a blue beret.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a MUP uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those -- stop, please. We see two people in camouflage. One pointing at the other. Can you tell us what they are?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by their outfit, they are members of the military police in the official uniforms of the VRS. They're wearing the uniforms that the VRS had at the time. And judging by the uniform and the belts they would be members of the military police. Whether they really were, I can't tell. But they could be, if we were to judge by the uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just see if we can see anybody that's worth. Pause there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not that easy to tell, but are you able to say what he is?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same kind of uniform as I saw just a minute ago. It's a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just see if there's anybody else that ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, pausing there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There's a man sitting there in white short sleeves with some kind of insignia on his shoulders, and there's another gentleman there sitting next to him. Can you say what they are?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the people. I haven't seen this video before. I don't know the people, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I don't know whether we get a closer view of the insignia. There are 1, 2, 3, 4, people in white short sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to assist at all, as to what they are?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they are. According to what I know, they are police members, members of the CSB. These are their uniforms. Otherwise, I don't know the persons that we can see in this still.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And let's just see if there's anybody else. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These two; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one closer to us or on the right could be a MP member. And the other, I don't know. He may have waited for transportation here. I don't know the man. But obviously he is wearing a uniform, but -- and if you want me to be specific, the uniform he is wearing was manufactured by the Svila company in Celinac, and it differs from the other uniform on the right. Because the army supplied itself from various sources. So one of the uniforms was manufactured by Svila, from Celinac, and the other by Jedinstvo from Vranje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have to say, sir, that is quite remarkable to be able to do that. All I want to ask is ask this: Is the chap in the middle with the moustache, are you saying he is ordinary military?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can -- the insignia on the left sleeve, I see for the first time now. Army members did not have such insignia. So on second thought he could be a member of the police if this patch reads "police," or milicija. Now can I see it and that is why I'm giving this answer. But he doesn't seem to be on duty because he isn't wearing a duty belt. I don't know who this man is, but what I said is based on this patch on his left sleeve.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I just want to see if the video focuses a little bit more on the man sitting down there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Having a look at him, sir, had you ever seen him before?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot be certain that I have ever seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have any dealings with any of the people who came from Banja Luka to the crime scene at Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's all I ask about that video. Could that short clip just be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I correctly understood, this video or any part of it is not the part of the 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think we have the ruling how -- how the -- how the exhibits are admitted on the 65 ter list first.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, and had it not arisen in this way, we would have made an application. But it's been disclosed. I cannot see any prejudice to the Defence in having this. And if anybody wants again to identify various people, it may be the gentleman sitting down will come of some relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And the witness's testimony is unintelligible without the video.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1672, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I have been reminded that the procedurally correct thing would be to, first of all, admit it to the exhibit list and then it would migrate into the body of evidence as a properly admitted exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I formally apply that the 10555 be admitted to our 65 ter list and then be admitted and marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the Defence raise an objection, if only for the record?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Because we know the ruling, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it is admitted to the exhibit list and then marked and admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right, sir, I want to just ask you a couple of questions about some documents you were shown again by Mr. Krgovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, before we go on. Mr. Witness, in one of the earlier questions - I'm not going to bother to go back to get the exact words that you used - that Ms. Korner put to you as to the -- when we were dealing with this video with the uniforms, you indicated something to the effect that you assumed they were army because of the uniforms that they -- because of what you observed. The -- was it possible in the region at the time for an individual, any individual to just go and purchase uniforms, particularly the camouflage variety; for instance, hunters and persons of -- of -- of that nature? I note, with interest, how you were able in one of your later answers looking at two individuals to identify the manufacturers from the different patterns of the -- of -- of the camouflage uniform. But I confess were it not for that answer I wouldn't have observed the difference myself. But my question is that -- really has to do with how much we can interfere from just looking at uniforms. Do you understand, or should I try to explain my question further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be specific. There were various types of uniforms out there, and they were readily available even at the factory that manufactured them. Initially, the Jedinstvo company from Vranje manufactured uniforms, military uniforms. That's the name of the company, Jedinstvo. In parallel, the -- the company named 22nd of December from Banja Luka also started manufacturing uniforms but they were buying the cloth from Pik Vranje. And again, parallel to that, Svila, from Celinac, also started manufacturing uniforms, so you could go there to the factory and buy a uniform. There were various kinds of uniforms as the situation developed. Uniforms were for sale, to be specific, at the Svila factory in Celinac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, just one clarification, believe the witness said the Svila, Celinac shop, not the factory. Maybe the witness can clarify slowly and then the -- the interpreters can properly interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Celinac, the town which is about 15 kilometres away from Banja Luka, there is a factory, or rather there was a factory called Svila. That was its name. There was also a factory outlet which was on the premises of the factory itself. Or you could buy their products, such as women's head-gear but also uniforms because they had a factory outlet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned Raif Alagic and what you described as his troops. Was Mr. Raif Alagic one of the defenders of Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you said you had all this information about him. Do you know what happened to him after the fall of -- the surrender of Vecici?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think I read about it in Sadikovic's book, in the third part. It says that he got killed. I think I found that information in the book. But I really don't know what happened to him. If you think that the information in the book is correct, then you can accept it, just as I did. Otherwise, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I can't give evidence one way or another and I haven't read Mr. Sadikovic's book. But what I'm trying to ask you about is you say that Mr. Alagic, as far as you were concerned, was this great big TO commander about whom you had a lot of information. But you weren't aware that he was in Vecici, and you weren't aware until you read Mr. Sadikovic's book that he had been killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I first got that information from that book. If I can remember correctly, it said that Raif Alagic got killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a couple of questions about some of the documents you were shown, I believe this time by Mr. Cvijetic. Document which was 1D00-3071. I think. Which may now be an exhibit. Or was already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. 2D119.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm reminded this is a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh. Then it shouldn't go on the screen. Oh. Not sure how to deal with this. I think it just shouldn't be shown on the screen. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked a number of questions about this document and in paragraph 2 the various people who were appointed to this particular police brigade. Was it you -- you who made those appointments -- this should be --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we go into private session. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Korner, this is a confidential document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... not on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 6 of this report, it says: "Due to being impossible to ensure the food for the brigade members who took under control the lines of the 3rd Battalion of the RSK police brigade ..." So was there a police brigade also from the -- the -- the Krajina -- the Republic of the Serb Krajina, which is, of course, over the border?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a kind of in-between land where there was also the police of the RSK that took part in cutting through the corridor. That unit was withdrawn, and that's why two platoons were supposed to take up positions in these two areas for reenforcement purpose.
