So, yes, that was a units that was left over from the breaking of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So all that I'm trying to get at is there was joint operation involving also the RSK police brigade.

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of the well-known operation of breaking open a corridor, and a number of units from the Republic of Serbian Krajina took part. A lot has been written about it, and there's nothing new to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then, finally, one of the last documents you were shown by Mr. Cvijetic, which is one of the combat reports. The last one that was exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't remember what the exhibit number was. It was the very last one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1D390. Thank you. Your Honour was there long before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were asked about the police brigade in Doboj. But I would like to look at the entry on the first page about half way down which says there have been armed conflicts in the Kotor Varos area. Where most of the enemy forces have been disarmed. And this is dated the 14th of June, three days after the takeover. Does that agree, because you were in the area of Kotor Varos during that time, does that accord with your recollection of events?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it, those are the events that were unfolding at the time, according to the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm concentrates on this. It says in this report, which I appreciate you say you haven't seen before: "Most of the enemy forces have been disarmed." And I'm asking you if that accords with your recollection of the situation on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-197 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not accord. This is a corps report. I don't know who wrote it and I don't know what that person meant by most of the enemy forces. It's a document that I did not write myself, and I can hardly give you an opinion on why it was written that way or who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But -- all right. Who would have provided to the author of this report which went out under General Talic's name to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could he answer that question, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he is one of the brigade's -- I'm sorry, are we in private session? No. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And I repeat for the record in open session what I would have said. You are now released as a witness and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we take the 20-minute break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one preliminary matter I would like to raise in respect to the coming witness. Namely, we received the -- late yesterday or actually this morning, I received the proofing note by our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor, and that proofing note on its first page, paragraph 4, and -- and 5 seems to suggest that the witness changed his position or his statement after the meeting with the -- or interview connected -- conducted by two Defence teams. However, Your Honours, the truth is the following: We met the -- and interviewed the witness at 2.15 on the 19th of -- of October. At the beginning of the interview, the witness had in his hand his statement given in 2004. He said that he was reviewing his statement that morning, and that statement contained in the margins already his comments and changes he intended to make. If I correctly remember, he said, I made the changes until the page 74. Because that was the time he had available that morning. And I said, I -- I specifically asked the witness, Did you made [sic] the Office of the Prosecutor aware that you -- that you are making the changes to your statement? He said, Yes. He said, I was talking -- I don't -- I don't -- I didn't ask whom he was talking to. He says, I was talking, I made them aware that there has been a number of changes in the statement while I was reviewing it. So the suggestion which is contained in the proofing note does not entirely correspond to the actual situation, how it happened. So, therefore, I suggest that my learned friend raise this with the -- with the witness once the witness is brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cvijetic -- Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, Ms. Korner and Mr. Sakic have left the courtroom, and I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith for the Prosecution. I'm not sure how to respond to this. The change that I'm most concerned with that the witness has brought to my attention when he came back and spoke with me on the 20th of October, relates to something that is at page, I think, 89 or 90, and the changes that he had made to his statement, he did not advise me of any of those changes that he made by handwriting in the margins until after he had met with the Defence for the first time. And I -- that's -- that's -- I'm only recounting what was told to me and the order in which those events occurred. If you want to hear anything further on that, I'm ready to address you, but I had one procedural matter that I wanted to raise before the witness is brought in, and I need to do that in private session. It relates to Witness ST-218 who was here, I think, last week.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, our next witness is Dobrislav Planojevic. He is Witness ST-220. And there are no protective measures requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Planojevic. First of all, do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your testimony. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out that the solemn declaration that are you about to make does expose you to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Now, then, would you please be kind enough to read aloud the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And, sir, could we begin by asking you to state your full name and your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dobrislav Planojevic, born 22nd August 1955, in Zakomo, near Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And what is your ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your profession today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inspector of quality control of the regional BH Pak [phoen], Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was your occupation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, is this your -- the first time you testified before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you ever testify in a court of your country about these matters, the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified before the State Court in BH, in the case Prosecutor against Lalovic and Skiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Very well. Let me then explain to you briefly how the proceedings unfold here in this Tribunal. You have been called as a witness by the Prosecution who is sitting to your right, and the Prosecutor asked, all together, for four hours, if I take the list we got, and five hours if I take the list of documents you provided with us, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I had drawn it from the original decision that it was five hours. Yes, I'm looking at, sorry, the decision of 22 July 2010, at page 10, ST-220. It says the Trial Chamber would allow five hours, but I would indicate to you I expect to take much less, more in the neighbourhood of three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. After the examination-in-chief, counsel for Mr. Stanisic, sitting to your left has asked for five hours as well to cross-examine you. And after that, the Zupljanin Defence will cross-examine you equally, but we didn't get any time estimate for that. Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, bearing in mind that my colleague Mr. Zecevic will conduct most of the cross-examination, we reserve the right to take half an hour, not more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic asked for six. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. When we are through all this, Mr. Planojevic, we'll give the floor back to the Prosecutor, who will have the probability to re-direct to put some more questions to you and after that, eventually, the Judges would have some questions, and we then would complete your testimony. As a practical matter, the recordings are taken on tape, and these tapes have to be changed all 90 minutes, so after 90 minutes, we take a 20-minute break, and we normally sit from -- from 9.00 to quarter to 2.00 every day. So, today, we still have three-quarters of an hour left for today's hearing. That's all I have to say. Thank you very much. And I'll give the floor to Mr. Hannis for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I begin my questions, I just want to state on the record one matter concerning logistics with this witness. He was advised of the possibility that we might not finish his evidence by the end of the day on Friday, earlier in the week. Now that seems quite likely, given the estimates and our late beginning time. At that time I had asked him when I thought that we would be resuming on Tuesday if he would want to stay the weekend and come back on Tuesday, et cetera. Now I understand we won't be resuming until Thursday next week and that may change his ideas about whether he wants to stay or go home, and I just say that out loud so he can be aware of it and discuss it with victim and witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Planojevic. I wanted to begin by asking you a little bit about your professional background. You told the Judges what you were doing in 1992. I guess it's fair to say that you, in your career, have been a professional policeman?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges about how that came to be, what education did you have, when did you do that, and briefly, if could you, tell us about the various police jobs you held from the start of your police work until 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can do that. I completed the secondary school for internal affairs in Sarajevo in 1973. I went on to the higher school for internal affairs in Belgrade, and that was in 1982 that I finished. And then I went to the Faculty of Security and Social Self-Protection, finishing in February 1986. After finishing secondary school in 1973, I started to work at the police station on traffic control duty in Sarajevo, and I did that until the 1st February 1974 which is when I moved to the city SUP, Sarajevo, taking up duties in crime prevention. I continued to work there until I left to attend higher school in 1979. Upon my return, I continued to work in the city SUP on duties involving elicit trade, or trafficking, until March 1982. I moved then to the Municipal Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Novo Sarajevo, again in crime prevention. On the 1st of January, 1984, I became assistant commander for crime prevention in the police station Novo Sarajevo, and I continued in that job until the 1st of February, 1985. From that time on, I was chief of crime prevention an investigation until September 1987. That is the time when I was assigned to become chief of public security in the same police station and stayed in that job until the 14th of April, 1984.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Municipality Assembly of Novo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, the interpretation of the dates when you held the job as chief of public security was recorded as being until the 14th of April, 1984. I suppose it would have been 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm -- I did not make a mistake. It was 1984. It's the same as written in the documents. Maybe you did not notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We saw that. But I thought that you would were going ahead chronologically in describing your career. That is why I was confused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I see correctly, I followed the chronology accurately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Planojevic. I think some of the confusion came earlier at page 68 you were recorded as saying that you were --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my mistake. It's not 1984; it's 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, that's when I became municipal secretary, because public security stations were called then Secretariat for Internal Affairs, and I became head of that secretariat of Novo Sarajevo. Towards the end of 1989, I remained practically in the same position but no longer as a secretary, but as chief of the public security station. It was just a change of name after the reorganisation. And until 1991, I remained chief of the Novo Sarajevo station. Early in June 1991, I became commander of the police station in Marin Dvor, which is Centar municipality and stayed there until the 4th of April, the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me stop you there and ask you a couple of questions after Mr. Zecevic says what he has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. Something was brought to my attention for the previous witness, and it concerns the media report by SENSE news agency and if we could go in the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, I should explain to you as a matter of courtesy that what just happened had nothing to do with you. It's just that the nature of a trial involves not only receiving testimony from a witness but very often procedural matters have to be dealt with by Trial Chamber. And it so happened that the matter with which we had to deal was one thing that had to be dealt with urgently. And because it did not concern your testimony at all, we thought it advisable that you be escorted from the courtroom. As I said, we intended no disrespect to you, and we apologise for the minor inconvenience. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic you had just told us about how you went from your position as chief of the Novo Sarajevo station to go to Marin Dvor. I think that's two words, Marin Dvor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in June 1991 as commander of the police station. As I understand the hierarchy, that -- that's not -- that would not be viewed as a promotion or even a lateral move; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us why that happened or your understanding of why that change took place?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections in the end of 1990, political parties already had quite some influence, as usual, and practically in all stations, there occurred changes in staffings. I was thinking about leaving the police altogether and registered a private company, because I was thinking, especially after seeing who became minister, that there wouldn't be much law in law enforcement anymore. The Law on Internal Affairs made it possible at the time, after 20 years of service with special credit in terms of pension, to retire. However, I did not succeed in that, and that's how I found myself commander in the Marin Dvor police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me follow up with a few questions about that. Before 1990, or before 1991, were you the member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the League of Communists up until 1990, I believe. I haven't been with any political party since, up to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah. And during that period before 1990, that was basically the party that anyone could be a member of?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Who replaced you in Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Milan Komljenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he have any prior police experience; do you know?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What work had he done before?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell. I know that he is a lawyer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was he a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, so I'd rather not answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said in your answer at page 71, line 5, that you were thinking about leaving the police altogether. Because you were thinking, especially after seeing who became minister, there wouldn't be much law in law enforcement anymore. The person who became minister that you're talking about there is Mr. Delimustafic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges why it is that you thought there wouldn't be much law in law enforcement anymore with him as minister?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I knew at the time about Delimustafic without any consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, briefly, if you can.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I knew the man from before. He used to be a police officer, and then he was dismissed from the police after a disciplinary -- after disciplinary proceedings. Then he engaged in private business. In an investigation in 1985 - police investigation - we worked on a case, and he was one of those arrested, as a result of that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Should I explain some more why he was arrested? I don't know if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a few specific questions perhaps. Did you personally have a role in the investigation that led to Mr. Delimustafic's arrest at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: When you lead an investigation involving a larger number of persons, the investigation took about half a year and five or six criminals were arrested. They were an organised group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do I take it by your answer that you actually led that investigation?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: It had to be under my control because it -- the launching of the investigation required my signature. I was chief at the time. And I directed the entire investigation. The terminology we used at the time was different so we didn't call it an investigation then. Dragisa Kujacic, Ismet Bajramovic, also known as Celo, and others were involved. During the execution, we were told by them that they were paid to set the car belonging to a detective on fire, a detective who used to prosecute them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of other specific questions. What was the general nature of the investigation? Was this public corruption, economic crime? How would you characterise it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you the following. There was a case of aggravated robbery, one rape, several instances of breaking and entering with theft - burglary, that is - and he was involved only due to the information that we received that he was the one who paid two others to set that car on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Was he specifically charged with a crime?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was charged and he was in detention for 30 days. I'm not sure how it -- how the case ended eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, do you know whether or not he was convicted?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could he have become the minister or the secretary of the interior if he had had a criminal conviction for a crime like that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Not under the law. But those were times when apparently anything was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was -- do you know, was Mr. Delimustafic aware, in 1991, that you had played a role in the investigation that led to his arrest and detention back in 1985?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's something I don't know either. You can believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the person that would have -- or could have approved your request to retire in 1991 or 1992, when you were thinking about it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Since it was already centralised, we all belonged to what was called secretariats of the interior then, the minister was in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you told us earlier you were not able to retire at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you complain to anyone about your demotion, or your move from being the chief in Novo Sarajevo to being the commander in Marin Dvor?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: This requires a broader explanation. So if you allow, I will explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, as briefly as you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: At a breakfast at the journalists' club, Vito Zepinic, the then-deputy minister; Momcilo Mandic, the then-assistant minister; and Mico Stanisic, secretary of the city SUP, and I met. In that conversation, since Vito was also in charge of personnel affairs on behalf of the Serb side practically, and the conversation was about my appointment as inspector for crime prevention and detection in the MUP HQ, Vito had earlier worked where I also had worked, in Novo Sarajevo, so we knew each other very well, it was promised to me then. But Kemo Sabovic informed me in mid-May that I was supposed to become commander at Marin Dvor. I went to pick up the decision to that effect, and I was dissatisfied. I gave Sabovic a short account of what had been agreed upon, and he advised me to go and see Zepinic again. I wasn't able to meet him. Allegedly, at the time he was present at a government meeting. On the following day, he also didn't answer my phone call, so I called up Momcilo Mandic, because it was clear at the time who was in charge of what, or who decided upon whose fate. For the Muslims there was Alija; for the Serbs, there was Vito and so on. Mandic received me. There was Bruno Stojic there, and they were having breakfast in his office. There was also Hilmo Selimovic. I also tried to convince them to appoint me, according to my wishes, because I didn't feel like going to Marin Dvor. Momo, in a half-joking manner - that was his way - he said, Just you go to Marin Dvor, you're a good Serb. Whereas, Selimovic made a comment as to -- made a comment that I had fared well as compared to some other old colleagues of ours who ended up somewhere in the outskirts, the periphery and that's how I went to Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From your earlier answer I understood you remained there until about the 4th of April, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Until about 10.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before I get into the details of that, were you aware of a dispatch that had been sent out by Momcilo Mandic, Mandic, on the 31st of March, calling on Serbs in the -- in the BiH MUP to -- to come join the newly created Serbian MUP? Did you see it or hear about it at that time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I know of the dispatch. It said that the Ministry of Interior would be divided into a Serb component and a Muslim, or Croatian, component, and that the headquarters would be at Vrace. That was around about the same time when the Cutileiro Plan about the possible cantonisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina was a topical affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you also aware that the -- the same day or shortly after the following day of Mr. Mandic's dispatch that Mr. Delimustafic sent out a dispatch telling employees of the Secretariat of the Interior that if they left to join a newly created MUP that they would lose their jobs in the current BiH Secretariat of Interior. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want, sir, to lie to you. I cannot be specific about that. I have a hard time remembering.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. On the 4th of April, at 10.30, you started to tell us about where you were and -- and what happened. Do you want to continue from that point?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can, but maybe it wouldn't make such sense unless I continue to say what had already happened by at that time. But I can continue, starting from the 4th. That's not a problem either. Because it's very important what preceded the 4th. Because that's more important than what actually happened on the 4th itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me -- let me make a request of you and advise you we have been in trial over a year. The Judges have heard a lot of evidence about what happened leading up to that time, and Defence counsel will have an opportunity to let you talk about that some. But because I have a time-limit on how much can I spend with you, for now, I would request, if you could tell me what happened on -- on April 4th. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Due to the overall situation, which had already become unsupportable, we - that is, the executives of the police station - would be on duty shifts for 24 hours. On the 4th of April, I was the duty officer at the Marin Dvor police station. Then Nedeljko Codo, a friend, called me up. Actually we were neighbours. We had neighbouring apartments at the seaside. We're not really good friends. He said to me that the Green Berets - that is, about half a dozen uniformed and armed persons - had -- had stolen his entire revenue from him. At that time, the amount involved was a couple of billion dinars, so you would have to convert it to know how much it is. But it was a large sum. It happened in the territory for which the police station of Marin Dvor had responsibility. I reacted by sending six or seven police officers to go to the site to try and find out what had happened and see whether they could find the perpetrators. One of the assistants, Suad Kadric, went along with the police officers. I received feedback from them that they were unable to find out anything, so I told them to return to the police station. When they arrived, they had a civilian with them. He was carrying an automatic rifle, a Kalashnikov rifle, as it was called. They briefed me that they had seen the man walking the streets with the rifle, which was not really a common sight, to put it very mildly, or actually it was inconceivable. That was at Kosevsko Brdo, that is a neighbourhood above the brickworks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where are we going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're going with the chronology of how he came to join the RS MUP. I can try and speed him along with some specific questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do. Because -- let's get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After speaking with this man, did you learn any information that caused you concern that something bigger than just one man walking around with a rifle was happening that night of April 4th?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: He was a Bosniak who stated that he had been issued a rifle at the Car pub on Kosevsko Brdo, and it was his task to secure the Centar municipality building with another nine men. And I asked him, Who could have give -- who could have given that you task? Because I'm the commander of the police station. That's my job. And he said to me that the president of the then-Executive Committee, the man's last name is Cengic, I'm not sure about his first name, that they were supposed to assemble in front of the -- that municipality building at 2200. Then it was clear to me that something unforeseen was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: And I immediately left the police station and asked a police officer, a Serb, to drive me home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that, did you attempt to get in contact with your fellow Serb police officers and -- and superiors in the area to learn what might be happening; and, if so, what did you find out?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: I first called out the Novo Sarajevo police station to check whether there was anything -- anything happened there, because I had been there long. I found out that nothing was happening there. Then I continued to my apartment. Upon arrival, the phone rang and I answered it, but nobody spoke on the other side. At one moment I was able to discern a typical noise produced by a radio station so I thought somebody was calling me from a police station. Then a voice said, Disconnect the line. And then it was disconnected. I called a couple of colleagues in some other police stations and inquired whether there was anything out of the ordinary, because I was asking myself whether I was imagining things, that there would be unwanted consequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I have been asked to alert you that there is a procedural matter we want to raise before we end the day. I don't know if you want to do it now or I can continue for a couple of minutes with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, we have to vacate this courtroom at 1.45. Mr. Planojevic, as was explained to you, your testimony will continue tomorrow. We have to raise shortly in order to make the courtroom available for another trial. I am to remind you that having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side and in such conversations as you may have persons outside of the courtroom, you cannot discuss your testimony in this trial. So the usher will now escort you from the courtroom while we deal with certain preliminary [sic] matters before we rise for the day in three minutes. Thank you, sir. Tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I'm sorry for that. I will try to speed up with the witness when we resume tomorrow. The issue I was asked to raise with you had to do with the adjudicated facts or the stipulations and agreed facts. Ms. Korner has indicated to me that there's -- we need some clarification about what you wanted filed. It's not only the ones pertaining to, I think, Visegrad, but to all the ones that we've reached prior to today, and I think that's our understanding but we wanted to say on the record to make sure it was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Aleksic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the instruction was the following: The Trial Chamber, therefore, directs the party first to file with the Chamber, no later than Friday of this week, a notice setting out in full the stipulations that have already been reached; for example, in relation to events in Visegrad. Now, my understanding -- I thought the very same that Your Honours would like that we -- that we combine everything, and on Wednesday we -- we give the full position of the Defence on each and every municipality or each and every adjudicated facts, except for the three that we have to give tomorrow. For the three witnesses, that -- that we need to give tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No. It would -- it would be helpful if all the -- the -- the facts that you are -- that you agreed upon, already, could be given to us so that we could work with -- with them before Wednesday eventually. If we could. We are in the dark here. So if -- unless that's too big an effort to ask, that's what we would like to have. Everything you already agreed upon. We -- we -- we understand, without knowing for sure, that there is already an agreement about Visegrad. Perhaps there are others. Can we have it, or is it a secret between parties until Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it is no secret between the parties. But the parties would appreciate if we could only have one motion and not a series of motions. That is actually our -- our suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you are -- you're talking about a motion. It's not a formal motion we need. It's just knowledge we need. We would like to know, not in the form of a formal motion. Can be a simple notice. Would that help?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry. I thought the instruction of yesterday was that we filed a joint motion of both parties or all three parties. That is what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Joint notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we will get a joint motion -- sorry, notice for tomorrow? Could it be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For -- for the three witnesses which are supposed to come next week, yes. Well, that was the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was the primary concern for us was to get any agreement we can about that so we can know for scheduling for next week. But I understand Judge Delvoie's desire to have all of them as soon as possible. I don't know how many there are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the trick is that the Chamber is also working to solve these issues and the more information we get, the more able we are to -- to start working on the remaining 92 bis witnesses. So it would be helpful to our work if we could have not only the three witnesses that are scheduled for next week, but also whatever other agreement you may have reached upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If this is not too much to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I anticipate that what you will get tomorrow is something less than what you'll get Wednesday, because hopefully Monday, Tuesday, the parties will have some additional ones beyond what we have so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the adjournment until 9.00 tomorrow morning.
